description:
Passwords are the one place in software where slow code is secure code and fast hashing is a catastrophic vulnerability. This video walks through why bcrypt, scrypt, and Argon2 deliberately burn CPU cycles and hoard memory to make offline brute-force attacks economically unfeasible.


0:00 The obsession with speed
0:52 Encryption vs hashing
1:17 Login flow: hash, then compare
1:43 SHA-256 was built for speed
2:06 GPUs: parallelism is the weapon
2:47 Fast hash = fast guessing
3:04 The solution: bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2
4:01 ASICs: hardware built to crack hashes
4:17 Memory hardness: the modern defense
5:15 Password security is economics

chapters.title: ASICs: hardware built to crack hashes

comments.author: @blacklistnr1

comments.text:
There are still ways to optimize speed without trashing security. First, if you have client-server architecture where the client uses the password to log in you can push hashing to the client and require 128-bit hash. Brute forcing anything 128-bit is impossible, so there's no vulnerability and the client being responsible for hashing decreases load on the server and potentially removes a DoS vulnerability.

Second, there was an interesting paper on a stretching algorithm that stretched the password as it was typed. Because typing the password takes time between the key strokes they used this to squeeze in some stretching. So to the user it looked faster even though it really took the same or even longer time.

You basically have to do a 2 step process where inputting the username already retrieves the salting string. Which also could leak that a specific user name exists.
On the plus side it does mean you aren't sending a clear text password over the Internet anymore.

comments.text: another option that a lot of systems use is an arbitrary wait period between attempts, and a lockout after a certain amount of failed attempts. It's obnoxious for the user sometimes, but significantly more effective at preventing brute force attacks than the hash algorithm itself. It also prevents another potential attack which measures the call and reponse time to predict which inputs are more or less accurate based on how quickly the server rejects the input, because all inputs will take the same amount of arbitrary time.
